title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Unlike with LLMs, the image generation market is a bit less competitive - there are many players, but they are not constantly breaking new ground, and some vendors haven't released a competitive model in many months. In this data from @ArtificialAnlys image arena, we can see model developments over time.
It might be the case that the standard diffusion technique is approaching its limits - the latest Google Imagen models are better, but the jump from 3 to 4 was only 18 Elo points, or 4 rankings. If not for a new technique in OpenAI's new viral model, we wouldn't have had all that much progress in the last 6-12 months.
Price is another thing that hasn't shifted all that much. Image generation is not orders of magnitude cheaper than it was ~2 years ago and is even more expensive for the best models.
I hope to see Google's answer to OpenAI's GPT-Image-1 soon, and maybe something great from @bfl_ml , who have been a bright spark in the last 12 months.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gwk4qZpWUAEgLCM.jpg

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
This chart shows the best image generation model at any given time, based on the @ArtificialAnlys arena and the model release dates.
A few points stand out:
- Massive gains from Dall-e 2 up to Midjourney 6.
- Arguably a slowdown in progress for diffusion models since then - Recraft wasn't dramatically better than a model from a year ago.
- A bigger shift occurred with GPT-4o, which is an auto-regressive + diffusion model.
- This shift doesn't fully capture GPT-4o’s capabilities in image editing and character consistency, which may be even more important than raw image quality.
- Price per image has remained around $0.02–$0.12 for most top models over the last three years. There's no clear downward trend; if anything, prices have increased slightly with GPT-4o.
Next, we should watch for responses from Google and other labs developing auto-regressive models. Clearly, this is a successful approach and has the potential to deliver even better quality at lower cost than what OpenAI currently offers.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GwpxsvlWsAAhTTZ.jpg

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Could GPT-5 be claimed to be 'AGI'? The funny thing about the OpenAI 'AGI clause' with Microsoft is that OpenAI needs to show it has developed 'systems' that have the 'capability' to generate $100bn in profits, not to actually generate the $100bn.
I am not saying they will do this, but I don't think it is completely out of the question that OpenAI could claim that to be true if you consider the following:
- OpenAI has already projected revenues (not profit) of $100bn in 2029; they could increase those projections following GPT-5.
- Gross margins are already at ~50%, expected to get to ~67% by 2028.
- The wording refers to 'system', not 'model', so they could claim GPT-5 to be the 'system' that would continue evolving. A bit like GPT-4 'system' evolved over 2-3 years.
- That system doesn't have to be just API or ChatGPT; it could be a platform for agents that could be making a lot more money in various verticals.
So putting this all together:
GPT-5 is a system capable of generating $100bn+ of gross profits (excl. training, research), over multiple years, as it evolves into more agentic, higher-value verticals, hence it is 'AGI'.
I know this is a little silly, so treat this more as a thought experiment than a prediction. The reason to look at this is that the relationship between OpenAI and Microsoft is getting a little tense, and if OpenAI managed to hold the 'it's AGI' gun over Microsoft's head (and hence Microsoft losing access to OpenAI IP), they might get more concessions out of them for the 'for profit' conversion.
Wording of the text & the numbers from @theinformation reporting

summary:
The most impactful thing about GPT-5 is not going to be the top tier of intelligence it will deliver (as much as I'm craving to see it), but rather the level of intelligence that free ChatGPT users will be able to access.
ChatGPT has around 700m weekly active users, and the vast majority of them do not pay. They have limited access to GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini. If the free version of GPT-5 is substantially better than GPT-4o and 4o-mini, then hundreds of millions of people will get an instant upgrade.
GPT-5 will be hugely important for that reason alone. I've been using o3 so much that I cannot possibly imagine going back to GPT-4o for everything, or even more so GPT-4o-mini.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
OpenAI and Anthropic both are showing pretty spectacular growth in 2025, with OpenAI doubling ARR in the last 6 months from $6bn to $12bn and Anthropic increasing 5x from $1bn to $5bn in 7 months.
If we compare the sources of revenue, the picture is quite interesting:
- OpenAI dominates consumer & business subscription revenue
- Anthropic just exceeds on API ($3.1bn vs $2.9bn)
- Anthropic's API revenue is dominated by coding, with two top customers, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, generating $1.4bn alone
- OpenAI's API revenue is likely much more broad-based
- Plus, Anthropic is already making $400m ARR from Code Claude, double from just a few weeks ago
My sense is that Anthropic's growth is extremely dependent on their dominance in coding - pretty much every single coding assistant is defaulting to Claude 4 Sonnet. If GPT-5 challenges that, with e.g. Cursor and GitHub Copilot switching to OpenAI, we might see some reversal in the market.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GxiSLfZXwAAdxGc.jpg

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary: The most boring and pointless discussions in AI, I find, are about definitions: can models "think"? Can they "reason"? What is AGI? What about ASI? The real answer is that AI is different from humans, and intelligence evolves in a different way. Any labels we put on it are proxies, a matter of context and opinion. We'll never get clear definitions for any of these things, so let's move on and stop wasting time.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
I ran a semi-scientific cost test of 3x top models: Opus 4.1 was 3x the cost of GPT-5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on real tasks.
I gave the same prompt to each model (with reasoning enabled) and looked at the cost, without normalising for tokens. The point was to capture real cost and not just the list price.
Some other observations:
- Opus 4.1 thinks very little; it is not really reasoning but rather planning, which doesn't take as many tokens
- GPT-5 was the only one to get the hard maths test correct
- The gap between Opus and others was the smallest for smaller tasks: 50% gap vs 85% gap for larger context tasks
- GPT-5 was the most likely to go overboard on reasoning tokens (especially in Coding): average of 8.5k vs Gemini 6k and Opus 3k in my tests
- In one test (not included here), I asked the models to write a 5k-word novel: Gemini and Opus ended up with ~3.5k words, and GPT-5 had 9.5k words
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GyG39mLXkAEI-V5.jpg

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Is everyone using Responses API when benchmarking GPT-5? I wonder if some benchmarks are underestimating GPT-5 if they are using the same Completions API format for all models
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GydDUsqWYAAXtRd.jpg
Quoting @shyamalanadkat
1/ lower costs: users have reported doubling cache hits from 40% to 80% on long rollout tasks with many tools; both reasoning and completion tokens can count towards cache utilization with responses API
2/ better reasoning: results in better reasoning performance; SWEbench score is ~4-5% higher with responses API than with chat completions on gpt-5
3/ encrypted reasoning: keep your workflow stateless while still benefiting from reasoning items
4/ stateful conversations: use store: true and previous_response_id to maintain context without resending the entire history

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
I was vaguely aware that OpenAI has a “priority” tier for lower latency, but I’d never seen benchmarks showing what you get for 2x the price. It turns out you can get about a 30-40% reduction in latency on the prompts I’ve tried.
I ran a (tiny) set of benchmarks - 10 queries per tier per prompt. One prompt was summarising a 7,000-word text (lots of input tokens) and another was writing a 1,000-word story (lots of output tokens).
Median latency dropped by 30-40%. There were other benefits too: time to first token was about 20-30% quicker, and variance was substantially lower as well (you can see the spread on the chart).
Is it worth 2x the price? I’m not selling it to you, and we haven’t switched any workloads yet, but it’s good to know this is an option.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gy-cguiWUAACm16.jpg

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Bitter lesson for coding assistants? We’ve seen a rise in terminal-based coding tools - Claude Code, OpenAI’s Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and others, including open-source efforts. Their success seems to boil down to ‘just let the model cook’, with fewer tricks and hacks - no embedding or editing models in between, or building on top of existing IDEs.
Obviously, asking a terminal to write code blindly isn’t the answer to all coding (yet), but it took me only a few prompts to get a dog-robot simulator running via Codex CLI with GPT-5. I’m not sure Lovable or Cursor would have done much better - and this was just part of my subscription.
If OpenAI adds this functionality to ChatGPT directly, you can imagine lots of regular users doing cool stuff themselves, without complex scaffolding or dedicated apps.
Just let the model cook.

summary:
OpenAI have updated Codex, turning it into a much more comprehensive coding system, which consists of:
1. Codex Terminal - a model running in your terminal
2. Codex IDE Extension (NEW) - you can add an extension to your IDE
3. Codex Cloud - an agent that spins up its own environment and runs in the cloud
4. Codex Code Review (NEW) - you can tag Codex to provide feedback on your code
Apart from the two new capabilities, we are seeing much tighter integration between these bits of the system. For example, you can already ask Code Review to fix issues, which then creates a Codex Cloud task, then you can use the IDE Extension to view the Cloud changes locally.
Not everything is perfectly aligned yet (e.g. you can't create Cloud tasks from your Terminal), and you can imagine them adding bits like an Agent to, e.g., test the UI of the changes - but the direction of travel is clear: you would be able to use an AI model to code in any modality you like, and coding workflows would be changing pretty rapidly very soon.

Quoting @merettm
Last week, our reasoning models took part in the 2025 International Collegiate Programming Contest (ICPC), the world’s premier university-level programming competition. Our system solved all 12 out of 12 problems, a performance that would have placed first in the world (the best human team solved 11 problems).
This milestone rounds off an intense 2 months of competition performances by our models:
- A second place finish in AtCoder Heuristics World Finals
- Gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad
- Gold medal at the International Olympiad in Informatics
- And now, a gold medal, first place finish at the ICPC World Finals.
I believe these results, coming from a family of general reasoning models rooted in our main research program, are perhaps the clearest benchmark of progress this year. These competitions are great self-contained, time-boxed tests for the ability to discover new ideas. Even before our models were proficient at simple arithmetic, we looked towards these contests as milestones of progress towards transformative artificial intelligence.
Our models now rank among the top humans in these domains, when posed with well-specified questions and restricted to ~5 hours. The challenge now is moving to more open-ended problems, and much longer time horizons. This level of reasoning ability, applied over months and years to problems that really matter, is what we’re after - automating scientific discovery.
This rapid progress also underscores the importance of safety & alignment research. We still need more understanding of the alignment properties of long-running reasoning models; in particular, I recommend reviewing the fascinating findings from the study of scheming in reasoning models that we released today (
Congratulations to my teammates that poured their hearts into getting these competition results, and to everyone contributing to the underlying fundamental research that enables them!

Morgan Stanley estimates that AI infrastructure will receive $2.9 trillion in funding through 2028, broken down as follows:
- $1.4tn: hyperscalers’ capex (e.g., Google, Meta, Oracle)
- $0.2tn: hyperscalers’ corporate debt
- $0.8tn: private credit (e.g., PIMCO, HPS)
- $0.15tn: asset-backed securities (ABS) & commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS)

The key point is risk concentration: if funding comes from hyperscalers’ cash, systemic impact is lower; if it’s debt or ABS/CMBS, the risk of cascading effects is higher. So far, debt hasn’t been the main source, but it is set to grow.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
"It works in practice - but does it work in theory?". My biggest problem with the criticism from the 'old guard' of AI (e.g. interview with Rich Sutton) is that there seems to be complete lack of engagement with what has been achieved in the last 2-3 years. The fact that we went from barely coherent snippets of code in 2022 to autonomous coding for many hours, must mean something.
It might be not the "theoretically correct" way to build the AGI but it is clearly a massive jump in capability that isn't showing signs of stopping. I wonder how many of the AI critics have actually meaningfully engaged with the latest models or have they just tried GPT-3.5 three years ago and left it at that?
Quoting @karpathy
Finally had a chance to listen through this pod with Sutton, which was interesting and amusing.
As background, Sutton's "The Bitter Lesson" has become a bit of biblical text in frontier LLM circles. Researchers routinely talk about and ask whether this or that approach or idea is sufficiently "bitter lesson pilled" (meaning arranged so that it benefits from added computation for free) as a proxy for whether it's going to work or worth even pursuing. The underlying assumption being that LLMs are of course highly "bitter lesson pilled" indeed, just look at LLM scaling laws where if you put compute on the x-axis, number go up and to the right. So it's amusing to see that Sutton, the author of the post, is not so sure that LLMs are "bitter lesson pilled" at all. They are trained on giant datasets of fundamentally human data, which is both 1) human generated and 2) finite. What do you do when you run out? How do you prevent a human bias? So there you have it, bitter lesson pilled LLM researchers taken down by the author of the bitter lesson - rough!
In some sense, Dwarkesh (who represents the LLM researchers viewpoint in the pod) and Sutton are slightly speaking past each other because Sutton has a very different architecture in mind and LLMs break a lot of its principles. He calls himself a "classicist" and evokes the original concept of Alan Turing of building a "child machine" - a system capable of learning through experience by dynamically interacting with the world. There's no giant pretraining stage of imitating internet webpages. There's also no supervised finetuning, which he points out is absent in the animal kingdom (it's a subtle point but Sutton is right in the strong sense: animals may of course observe demonstrations, but their actions are not directly forced/"teleoperated" by other animals). Another important note he makes is that even if you just treat pretraining as an initialization of a prior before you finetune with reinforcement learning, Sutton sees the approach as tainted with human bias and fundamentally off course, a bit like when AlphaZero (which has never seen human games of Go) beats AlphaGo (which initializes from them). In Sutton's world view, all there is is an interaction with a world via reinforcement learning, where the reward functions are partially environment specific, but also intrinsically motivated, e.g. "fun", "curiosity", and related to the quality of the prediction in your world model. And the agent is always learning at test time by default, it's not trained once and then deployed thereafter. Overall, Sutton is a lot more interested in what we have common with the animal kingdom instead of what differentiates us. "If we understood a squirrel, we'd be almost done".
As for my take...
First, I should say that I think Sutton was a great guest for the pod and I like that the AI field maintains entropy of thought and that not everyone is exploiting the next local iteration LLMs. AI has gone through too many discrete transitions of the dominant approach to lose that. And I also think that his criticism of LLMs as not bitter lesson pilled is not inadequate. Frontier LLMs are now highly complex artifacts with a lot of humanness involved at all the stages - the foundation (the pretraining data) is all human text, the finetuning data is human and curated, the reinforcement learning environment mixture is tuned by human engineers. We do not in fact have an actual, single, clean, actually bitter lesson pilled, "turn the crank" algorithm that you could unleash upon the world and see it learn automatically from experience alone.
Does such an algorithm even exist? Finding it would of course be a huge AI breakthrough. Two "example proofs" are commonly offered to argue that such a thing is possible. The first example is the success of AlphaZero learning to play Go completely from scratch with no human supervision whatsoever. But the game of Go is clearly such a simple, closed, environment that it's difficult to see the analogous formulation in the messiness of reality. I love Go, but algorithmically and categorically, it is essentially a harder version of tic tac toe. The second example is that of animals, like squirrels. And here, personally, I am also quite hesitant whether it's appropriate because animals arise by a very different computational process and via different constraints than what we have practically available to us in the industry. Animal brains are nowhere near the blank slate they appear to be at birth. First, a lot of what is commonly attributed to "learning" is imo a lot more "maturation". And second, even that which clearly is "learning" and not maturation is a lot more "finetuning" on top of something clearly powerful and preexisting. Example. A baby zebra is born and within a few dozen minutes it can run around the savannah and follow its mother. This is a highly complex sensory-motor task and there is no way in my mind that this is achieved from scratch, tabula rasa. The brains of animals and the billions of parameters within have a powerful initialization encoded in the ATCGs of their DNA, trained via the "outer loop" optimization in the course of evolution. If the baby zebra spasmed its muscles around at random as a reinforcement learning policy would have you do at initialization, it wouldn't get very far at all. Similarly, our AIs now also have neural networks with billions of parameters. These parameters need their own rich, high information density supervision signal. We are not going to re-run evolution. But we do have mountains of internet documents. Yes it is basically supervised learning that is ~absent in the animal kingdom. But it is a way to practically gather enough soft constraints over billions of parameters, to try to get to a point where you're not starting from scratch. TLDR: Pretraining is our crappy evolution. It is one candidate solution to the cold start problem, to be followed later by finetuning on tasks that look more correct, e.g. within the reinforcement learning framework, as state of the art frontier LLM labs now do pervasively.
I still think it is worth to be inspired by animals. I think there are multiple powerful ideas that LLM agents are algorithmically missing that can still be adapted from animal intelligence. And I still think the bitter lesson is correct, but I see it more as something platonic to pursue, not necessarily to reach, in our real world and practically speaking. And I say both of these with double digit percent uncertainty and cheer the work of those who disagree, especially those a lot more ambitious bitter lesson wise.
So that brings us to where we are. Stated plainly, today's frontier LLM research is not about building animals. It is about summoning ghosts. You can think of ghosts as a fundamentally different kind of point in the space of possible intelligences. They are muddled by humanity. Thoroughly engineered by it. They are these imperfect replicas, a kind of statistical distillation of humanity's documents with some sprinkle on top. They are not platonically bitter lesson pilled, but they are perhaps "practically" bitter lesson pilled, at least compared to a lot of what came before. It seems possibly to me that over time, we can further finetune our ghosts more and more in the direction of animals; That it's not so much a fundamental incompatibility but a matter of initialization in the intelligence space. But it's also quite possible that they diverge even further and end up permanently different, un-animal-like, but still incredibly helpful and properly world-altering. It's possible that ghosts:animals :: planes:birds.
Anyway, in summary, overall and actionably, I think this pod is solid "real talk" from Sutton to the frontier LLM researchers, who might be gear shifted a little too much in the exploit mode. Probably we are still not sufficiently bitter lesson pilled and there is a very good chance of more powerful ideas and paradigms, other than exhaustive benchbuilding and benchmaxxing. And animals might be a good source of inspiration. Intrinsic motivation, fun, curiosity, empowerment, multi-agent self-play, culture. Use your imagination.

Sora 2 is not just a 'video model', it’s a 'narrative model'.
The difference between meaningless AI slop and engaging short-form videos is the narrative - this is what Sora gets right. It is the first model that generates short narratives by combining an often funny script with the audio and video - all from a short text prompt from the user.
This pretty funny clip is one of my favourites that I've generated, I haven't asked for any of this script, but it makes sense and it made me laugh.
In comparison, take this output from Veo 3 - its video and audio quality are superb, but it lacks any narrative. It just puts audio and video together into a package, but the narrative still needs to come from the user.
My prediction is that Sora 2 will do amazingly well with casual users, but more experienced AI video creators may not like it, as you end up giving a lot of control to Sora instead of crafting the video yourself.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
My short essay on LLMs & AGI:
Have we reached the 'AGI of flight'?
Not even close. Our planes can carry hundreds of passengers across the globe in just a few hours, yet nothing we build matches a godwit flying non-stop for eleven days without rest or the agility of a bat navigating in complete darkness.
In 1903, scientist Simon Newcomb declared heavier-than-air flight impossible. Two months later, the Wright brothers flew at Kitty Hawk.
Today's debate over LLMs and AGI feels similar. LLMs, like planes, might never replicate every nuance of the human mind, but they might not have to. Commercial aviation never matched the godwit but transformed civilization, carrying millions across the world every day.
LLMs could do even more. Intelligence shapes every interaction, every piece of information, every decision. Flight changed how we move; intelligence will reshape how we think.
The Wright brothers didn’t need to beat the godwit.

Nvidia's GB200 is a beast on all dimensions - raw performance, price vs performance or tokens per megawatt.

Dylan and the @SemiAnalysis_ team did an amazing job on this benchmark, which they say will run for a very long time so we can track improvements in performance as they arise.

How many Tokens are generated per MW of capacity on different infrastructure?

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
It feels obvious to me that the only workable learning mechanic must be self-reflection & deliberate learning - looking at the experience and deciding what to learn and what to discard.
It would be some combination of getting external reward (e.g. human telling them it was wrong and why) and being smart enough to understand if you did the right thing.
One problem is that models are not smart enough to be good judges - they have bad taste and they don't understand what's important vs not.
For example, take a look at the ChatGPT memories, to me 90% is random nonsense and my jailbreak attempts from a year ago - model should have been smart enough to understand it shouldn't be memorising those.
So yes, we absolutely need pre-training (smart model), RL (to learn from interactions), but we need a breakthrough on self-reflection and deliberate learning - this does not work yet.
Quoting @karpathy
My pleasure to come on Dwarkesh last week, I thought the questions and conversation were really good.
I re-watched the pod just now too. First of all, yes I know, and I'm sorry that I speak so fast :). It's to my detriment because sometimes my speaking thread out-executes my thinking thread, so I think I botched a few explanations due to that, and sometimes I was also nervous that I'm going too much on a tangent or too deep into something relatively spurious. Anyway, a few notes/pointers:
AGI timelines. My comments on AGI timelines looks to be the most trending part of the early response. This is the "decade of agents" is a reference to this earlier tweet Basically my AI timelines are about 5-10X pessimistic w.r.t. what you'll find in your neighborhood SF AI house party or on your twitter timeline, but still quite optimistic w.r.t. a rising tide of AI deniers and skeptics. The apparent conflict is not: imo we simultaneously 1) saw a huge amount of progress in recent years with LLMs while 2) there is still a lot of work remaining (grunt work, integration work, sensors and actuators to the physical world, societal work, safety and security work (jailbreaks, poisoning, etc.)) and also research to get done before we have an entity that you'd prefer to hire over a person for an arbitrary job in the world. I think that overall, 10 years should otherwise be a very bullish timeline for AGI, it's only in contrast to present hype that it doesn't feel that way.
Animals vs Ghosts. My earlier writeup on Sutton's podcast . I am suspicious that there is a single simple algorithm you can let loose on the world and it learns everything from scratch. If someone builds such a thing, I will be wrong and it will be the most incredible breakthrough in AI. In my mind, animals are not an example of this at all - they are prepackaged with a ton of intelligence by evolution and the learning they do is quite minimal overall (example: Zebra at birth). Putting our engineering hats on, we're not going to redo evolution. But with LLMs we have stumbled by an alternative approach to "prepackage" a ton of intelligence in a neural network - not by evolution, but by predicting the next token over the internet. This approach leads to a different kind of entity in the intelligence space. Distinct from animals, more like ghosts or spirits. But we can (and should) make them more animal like over time and in some ways that's what a lot of frontier work is about.
On RL. I've critiqued RL a few times already, e.g. . First, you're "sucking supervision through a straw", so I think the signal/flop is very bad. RL is also very noisy because a completion might have lots of errors that might get encourages (if you happen to stumble to the right answer), and conversely brilliant insight tokens that might get discouraged (if you happen to screw up later). Process supervision and LLM judges have issues too. I think we'll see alternative learning paradigms. I am long "agentic interaction" but short "reinforcement learning" I've seen a number of papers pop up recently that are imo barking up the right tree along the lines of what I called "system prompt learning" , but I think there is also a gap between ideas on arxiv and actual, at scale implementation at an LLM frontier lab that works in a general way. I am overall quite optimistic that we'll see good progress on this dimension of remaining work quite soon, and e.g. I'd even say ChatGPT memory and so on are primordial deployed examples of new learning paradigms.
Cognitive core. My earlier post on "cognitive core": , the idea of stripping down LLMs, of making it harder for them to memorize, or actively stripping away their memory, to make them better at generalization. Otherwise they lean too hard on what they've memorized. Humans can't memorize so easily, which now looks more like a feature than a bug by contrast. Maybe the inability to memorize is a kind of regularization. Also my post from a while back on how the trend in model size is "backwards" and why "the models have to first get larger before they can get smaller"
Time travel to Yann LeCun 1989. This is the post that I did a very hasty/bad job of describing on the pod: . Basically - how much could you improve Yann LeCun's results with the knowledge of 33 years of algorithmic progress? How constrained were the results by each of algorithms, data, and compute? Case study there of.
nanochat. My end-to-end implementation of the ChatGPT training/inference pipeline (the bare essentials)
On LLM agents. My critique of the industry is more in overshooting the tooling w.r.t. present capability. I live in what I view as an intermediate world where I want to collaborate with LLMs and where our pros/cons are matched up. The industry lives in a future where fully autonomous entities collaborate in parallel to write all the code and humans are useless. For example, I don't want an Agent that goes off for 20 minutes and comes back with 1,000 lines of code. I certainly don't feel ready to supervise a team of 10 of them. I'd like to go in chunks that I can keep in my head, where an LLM explains the code that it is writing. I'd like it to prove to me that what it did is correct, I want it to pull the API docs and show me that it used things correctly. I want it to make fewer assumptions and ask/collaborate with me when not sure about something. I want to learn along the way and become better as a programmer, not just get served mountains of code that I'm told works. I just think the tools should be more realistic w.r.t. their capability and how they fit into the industry today, and I fear that if this isn't done well we might end up with mountains of slop accumulating across software, and an increase in vulnerabilities, security breaches and etc.
Job automation. How the radiologists are doing great and what jobs are more susceptible to automation and why.
Physics. Children should learn physics in early education not because they go on to do physics, but because it is the subject that best boots up a brain. Physicists are the intellectual embryonic stem cell I have a longer post that has been half-written in my drafts for ~year, which I hope to finish soon.
Thanks again Dwarkesh for having me over!

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
LLMs suck at being judges & have poor taste - this is a huge blocker for both practical applications and training.
On the practical side:
- Quality - 'is this a good quality output?'
- Working agents - 'have I reached the goal or should I keep going?'
- Memory - 'should I remember this about the user/project?'
On the training side:
- Synthetic data generation - 'is this valuable data?'
- Deliberate learning - 'would this be useful for me to know?'
- In-process learning - 'am I making progress?'
All of these things sort of work a bit, but nowhere near the level they need to. The number of times I've had an LLM create a chart with messed-up labels and fail to even recognise what's wrong is pretty shocking.
I don't know if this ability would naturally emerge, but I'm guessing labs could make progress by explicitly training for this 'judge' ability, which doesn't seem too hard and should speed up their research quite a bit.

What I like and don't like about OpenAI's Atlas browser. This is the biggest (potential) assault on Google, but ultimately a bit raw.
Good:
- Nice UI, lightweight, easy to switch from Chrome
- Agent mode UI is cool
- It can search your browsing history
- It can look at all of your tabs
- Agent mode is in the same environment as you & can use your logins - big unlock
Not so good:
- Side bar doesn't have a model picker yet, so you are stuck with non-thinking GPT-5
- I generally don't like the use cases like 'write this for me' or 'what's written on this page' - feels a bit ai-sloppy
- Agent mode is still a bit painful & slow
Ultimately, apart from the early version agent mode, there's not huge amount in it. There's not magical voice mode that let's you interact with the web differently, or some other AI-pilled ideas (ChatGPT side bar isn't it).
But, if it does get better, the biggest threat to Google is that new tab opens ChatGPT and not Google search. There's no guarantee, but as Chrome took over the browser market some years back, so could a new browser. And if this happens, Google will lose some default surfaces they benefited from greatly.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
I'm very down on the idea of running local models on smartphones. OSS 20b is a model you can barely run on a good laptop, yet it ranks 93rd on LMArena.
Users can access GPT-5-Chat for free via the ChatGPT app which ranks 10th. It would take at least a couple of years of algorithmic and hardware improvements to get an OSS 20b-like model running on a phone, and by then cloud models will be even further ahead.
As a user, I'm forced to spend more money on a more expensive phone and sacrifice battery life just to get a sloppy "summarise this email" response from a 3b local model. Google's Pixel phones are falling victims to this already.
For $200 you might pay for an 'AI phone' you can get over 10k+ (!) ChatGPT conversations at GPT-5-Chat API prices. That's 5 years worth of 5x conversations a day. Privacy isn't a real concern either - people already use cloud services regularly for far more sensitive things than ChatGPT conversations (for example, Gmail, Google Photos).
Apple's dream of accelerating the renewal cycles because people would want to get a 4b model instead of a 3b model with the latest iPhone is not realistic, as long as you can get access to a 1 trillion model in the cloud for free.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
What's a realistic path for open source models? xAI models will be 8 trillion parameters, all big labs are investing hundreds of billions in infra, meaning that a multi-billion training run would be pretty common.
Even if we get some of these models open sourced, nobody could reasonably run them apart from large professional independent clouds (Coreweave, Nebius etc.), but what's the business model here - Qwen spends a billion and hands it over to others to run without any fees?
The bet for open source is essentially anti-AGI, that reasonably sized models will keep being good enough and all of that training infrastructure is not going to really ever pay off.
Or that there will be super intelligent models, but there'll always be room for cheaper and smaller models to do some tasks.
It feels to me like we are reaching a crunch point with open source models, competitive-ish models like Kimi K2 or Ernie are 1-2 trillion parameters, they are not really available super widely. Business model for them seems to be 1st party inference, which is a difficult moat to sustain when you are handing over the weights. I'd be curious to see where open source be next year, would it keep up? Or get somewhat stuck and this size and try to out innovative in efficiency?

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Having played with Nano-Banana-Pro, I must say, I'm a little disappointed. It is a model that takes several times longer and is backed by a very competent Gemini 3 Pro, but:
- Instruction following is poor, I need to spell things out for it to work
- Sometimes it jumps on a word and is being too literal
- In transforming images it still does this weird thing of cropping and adding the image directly rather than actually transforming it
- Reliability is low, often need to regenerate multiple times to get something good
So when you are seeing spectacular outputs, I would bet that vast majority of them required quite a lot of re-generations and tinkering with the prompts.
One area where it seems to be unambiguously better is rendering large amounts of text and perhaps for realistic images.
But if you compare the original nano-banana to the new one side by side (e.g. on the Arena) as I did, I bet you would actually prefer the original one quite often. So still all to play for in the image space.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
My (speculative) assessment of OpenAI's path, current state & the future:
OpenAI:
- Right now its 'thinking' model is a lot stronger than anyone else's, while 'non-thinking' model is clearly lagging behind
- OpenAI discovered o1's inference time compute scaling and changed direction rapidly
- This was quite a change from the 'scaling pre-train' lab to a 'RL' lab
- All of the base models for o-series and GPT-5 models are probably trained at a similar level to GPT-4 (Epoch's estimates are showing this too)
- This means that they haven't meaningfully scaled pre-training for 2.5 years (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1 etc. were all optimisations)
- In parallel, GPT-4.5 was the big new pre-train, released 2 years after GPT-4 in March 2025 and OpenAI had big hopes for it
- But, as GPT-4.5 was sort of a flop and thinking models were so much more impressive, with faster iteration cycles, any new big pre-trains got de-prioritised
- So GPT-5, 5.1, 5.1-codex etc were all based on probably a new pre-train, maybe a bit bigger than GPT-4, but definitely smaller than GPT-4.5
Google & Anthropic:
- In the meantime, Google and Anthropic haven't worked out the 'reasoning' paradigm (they scrambled after o1-preview) and hence continued refining & scaling pre-training
- They have slapped on reasoning subsequently, but it is nowhere near as advanced as OpenAI's (e.g. Claude Opus 4.5 SWE bench scores are the same with thinking and without)
- But, their non-reasoning models are miles ahead of the non-reasoning GPT-5. There's no comparison between Sonnet/Opus 4.5 and GPT-5 without reasoning.
Going forward:
- OpenAI is reaching a point where long thinking times become unusable for day to day work, e.g. 10-15 mins for a coding task when Gemini or Claude can do it in 2, eliminates them from a lot of the market, even if the final answer is better
- Very hard scientific problems will benefit from OpenAI's approach (you can see them talk about science a lot), but this is not where the market is and I don't know how OpenAI can capture the upside of discoveries, if they ever come
- The question is - does OpenAI have a better pre-train in the back pocket or not? If they do, their response could be fast & mighty
- If they don't and they have to start now, it would be 6 months+ before we get a big response from OpenAI - 3-4 months for pre-train, 2-3 months for RL, safety etc.
- The biggest edge I see for OpenAI is for them to leverage their excellent long thinking models for synthetic data generation
- If they could run models for 5-10-24 hours to get the best data & feed it back to the pre-train, their new base model could be as impressive as Anthropic's & Google's combined
- Then, imagine Opus 4.5 base + GPT-5-thinking/pro level reasoning, it would be really quite something

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Short timelines & AGI = 'automate all remote work' idea comes from underestimating what other people do. It is very common for people to imagine that it is easy to automate other people's jobs but not your own.
From your perspective, you shoot off an email and the thing gets done. But when you do your job, you see 100s of inconsistencies you need to manage or judgements you need to make.
Then remember, that automating all remote work doesn't just mean call centre workers. It means theoretical physicists, forensic accountants, biostatisticians, movie producers, therapists, urban planners or start-up founders.
I think a more practical and perhaps interim 'AGI' level could be 'automating all identifiable tasks' which feels more achievable in the next 5 years, doesn't imply mass unemployment/take off scenarios and makes the timeline debate more grounded.

The whole anti-ad sentiment in ChatGPT is crazy, ads are good.
- if you don't want ads you can pay, like you do with YouTube, Spotify or Netflix

- the only reason why Meta and buy 500k GPUs is because of ads

- if you want openai to finance the massive build out, they will have to have ads
- $100bn revenue without ads is extremely difficult to imagine, especially if you assume they Anthropic would do well in b2b & coding, which they are winning now
All of this smacks of elitism, "I can afford to pay so we shouldn't have a free version". Let people choose, as long as you can pay your way out of having ads, I don't see any it should bother anyone.
I really kills me that, especially before gpt-5, vast majority of the experiences that people had with AI were awful slop models. We should want for AI companies to have strong independent business models and not rely on investor sentiment for the next round.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
I've posed a question: "Does OpenAI have a better pre-train in the back pocket or not?" and looks like the answer from Mark Chen is "Yes" - so we should expect a big response from OpenAI before the end of the year.
@markchen90, OpenAI Head of Research:
- "In the last 2 years we've put so much resourcing into, into reasoning and one byproduct of that is you lose a little bit of muscle on pre training and post training."
- "In the last six months, @merettm and I have done a lot of work to build that muscle back up."
- "With all the focus on RL, there's an alpha for us because we think there's so much room left in pre training."
- "As a result of these efforts, we've been training much stronger models. And that also gives us a lot of confidence carrying into Gemini 3 and other releases coming this end of the year."
So it does look like my assessment was broadly correct and they were neglecting pre-training quite a bit. The good news is that they've spent the last 6 months building that up and the big response shouldn't be too far away.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1995744232049704965/img/Y7kUeAT5uXtbkqjw.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/1995744232049704965/vid/avc1/480x270/7GorvWKid9PxrcDh.mp4?tag=21
Quoting @petergostev
My (speculative) assessment of OpenAI's path, current state & the future:
OpenAI:
- Right now its 'thinking' model is a lot stronger than anyone else's, while 'non-thinking' model is clearly lagging behind
- OpenAI discovered o1's inference time compute scaling and changed direction rapidly
- This was quite a change from the 'scaling pre-train' lab to a 'RL' lab
- All of the base models for o-series and GPT-5 models are probably trained at a similar level to GPT-4 (Epoch's estimates are showing this too)
- This means that they haven't meaningfully scaled pre-training for 2.5 years (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1 etc. were all optimisations)
- In parallel, GPT-4.5 was the big new pre-train, released 2 years after GPT-4 in March 2025 and OpenAI had big hopes for it
- But, as GPT-4.5 was sort of a flop and thinking models were so much more impressive, with faster iteration cycles, any new big pre-trains got de-prioritised
- So GPT-5, 5.1, 5.1-codex etc were all based on probably a new pre-train, maybe a bit bigger than GPT-4, but definitely smaller than GPT-4.5
Google & Anthropic:
- In the meantime, Google and Anthropic haven't worked out the 'reasoning' paradigm (they scrambled after o1-preview) and hence continued refining & scaling pre-training
- They have slapped on reasoning subsequently, but it is nowhere near as advanced as OpenAI's (e.g. Claude Opus 4.5 SWE bench scores are the same with thinking and without)
- But, their non-reasoning models are miles ahead of the non-reasoning GPT-5. There's no comparison between Sonnet/Opus 4.5 and GPT-5 without reasoning.
Going forward:
- OpenAI is reaching a point where long thinking times become unusable for day to day work, e.g. 10-15 mins for a coding task when Gemini or Claude can do it in 2, eliminates them from a lot of the market, even if the final answer is better
- Very hard scientific problems will benefit from OpenAI's approach (you can see them talk about science a lot), but this is not where the market is and I don't know how OpenAI can capture the upside of discoveries, if they ever come
- The question is - does OpenAI have a better pre-train in the back pocket or not? If they do, their response could be fast & mighty
- If they don't and they have to start now, it would be 6 months+ before we get a big response from OpenAI - 3-4 months for pre-train, 2-3 months for RL, safety etc.
- The biggest edge I see for OpenAI is for them to leverage their excellent long thinking models for synthetic data generation
- If they could run models for 5-10-24 hours to get the best data & feed it back to the pre-train, their new base model could be as impressive as Anthropic's & Google's combined
- Then, imagine Opus 4.5 base + GPT-5-thinking/pro level reasoning, it would be really quite something

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
My problems with ChatGPT for any PMs looking what to do during the 'code red' situation (long list just features, not models, android user, pro subscriber):
Android app has really deteriorated:
- Android app takes several seconds to remember what model I used before, so I end up sending simple queries to Pro or hard queries to Auto all the time
- When sharing the image to the android app it doesn't attach in a way that uses vision, but instead it does OCR with python. I need to attach image from the chat for it to work
- Thinking doesn't work in the background like pro, why do I need to keep my chat active for minutes at a time?
- Pro doesn't send notifications half the time when it's done - I've got so many dead queries that I sent and forgot I did
- Constant weirdness with connection - I never know if things are done or not, sometimes things break and no response given
- is the response done? To check I need to refresh, but to refresh I need to go to all charts and drag it from there rather than in the chat
- I still can't manage tasks from the app, I have some going back a year that I forget to switch off
Web app & other:
- what happened to canvas? It was a nice feature no preview button stopped working and it is a buggy mess
- Custom GPTs is a nice feature for business but it has no love for the last 2 years and that whole line has died out - non technical users are not vibe coding, they have nothing else 2 years on. Agent builder is not in chatgpt and is hard to use for non technical people
- voice is transcription is not reliable apart from short recordings, probably the connection issue again, I'm too afraid to use it after losing several minutes of voice notes
- the whole connection issue and thinking not giving outputs is just abysmal, it has to get better
- data analyst is still very janky - you can upload only limited files, it breaks half the time, it is a huge use case for business but non-Codex users are stuck in 2023. I'm basically recommending people don't use chatgpt for data analysis anymore
- we are still stuck with different experiences depending on what file you upload how, you need to be an expert in knowing how chatgpt treats different files to use it properly
- I don't use the mac app that much but understand it is behind on many features now (eg group chats)
That's everything I could think of now. I know AI is fast moving and it is hard to keep everything going. And maybe I'm a dumb android user and things are better on the other side, but I hope the 'code red' won't be just get another model iteration out but actually go back to caring about the core ChatGPT experience

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Biggest clearest blocker I see for agents is that they are terrible at self-reflection & at being judges and I don't see that later models are getting better at this.
Without being able to judge 'this this good?' there's no hope we will get agents that actually work well without constant human input.
It is not even just about the 'taste' of a senior experienced professional - models miss such obvious issues (e.g. extra limbs, UI overlaps, bad textures, bad user flows).
Even if they do spot the issues, they have poor judgement about what issues are actually important - something that any human would jump to instantly, they focus on trivial things and list the obvious hole as number 6.
Part of it could be poor vision capabilities, but I think it is beyond that too - they just don't seem to connect the dots that are obvious to humans.
I imagine labs need to deliberately train models to 'judge' - I don't know if it is just a post training tweak or it is a more fundamental part of the 'brain' missing. Code review is a step towards this, but somehow it doesn't seem to generalise enough.
My pet theory is that we train models to be 'helpful assistants' and they have had time judging if they need to be subservient. Who is training the a**hole manager model?

Sharing my experience of using GPT-5.2's new Extra-High thinking mode - which sometimes takes 1-2 hours to think & respond. I've tested it on the much more advanced version of the 'Golden Gate Bridge' prompt. It produced by far the best output I've ever had.
TL;DR:
- It is the first model that can really work for hours at a time
- It is the most reliable / coherent model I've tried (e.g. doesn't screw up other parts of the code)
- But, it is still not perfect at one-shotting different tasks
- Codex needs a bit more optimisation, e.g. with effective planning to make sure that all tasks get completed
Overall, I'd say it is more of an experiment right now than a practical way to use these models. But it is a nice glimpse into the future - if these models can actually solve tasks reliably, and if they do take an hour or two to do so, it might not be a problem. But we are not quite there yet.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
The best early application of continuous learning is your personal LLM-as-a-judge.
Imagine an LLM that knows exactly how you code, write emails, what you consider to be 'good' legal document or what is a good design - anything that you normally give feedback to LLMs on is aligned to your preferences.
Right now even best LLMs are hopeless at this task - they lack judgement and are not aligned to you at all. But the moment you have a judge that gets you and it can autonomously give feedback to other LLMs about how to do better, you don't need to personalise all LLMs out there. You can just have your personal judge that follows you from Cursor to Claude Code, or from Figma to Adobe Illustrator, or from Slack to Gmail.
This would be far simpler to implement too, it would be worthwhile to spend a few hundred dollars and some effort personalising one LLM judge than expecting some new dynamic LLMs architecture to emerge everywhere.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
The big reason why people choose better models isn’t so much IQ points, but reliability. This is why smaller models often suck - it isn’t that they literally can’t do the task, but that they don’t do it anywhere near reliably enough.
If you used Sonnet 3.5 back in the day, and you tried hard enough, you could output great code. But occasionally it would completely destroy your app or production database.
Then you get this cascading churn effect:
- Some people got unlucky and never adopted it (the "AI sucks" group)
- Some people are not skilled or knowledgeable enough to build safeguards, so they play with it and then leave
- And then you have developers who spend many weeks working out ways to make it reliable (scaffolding, retries, judges, sandboxes, rollbacks, etc.)
I remember building a relatively simple LLM-based classification system where we used GPT-4o back then. I was tearing my hair out over how unreliable it was, again not that it couldn’t do the job, but that it would screw up too often. To counter that, we had to build a complex multi-step system to make sure it couldn’t make these mistakes (triaging, best-of-three, LLM as a judge, etc.). I bet that if we used any of the more recent LLMs, we’d build the same app in a single step and move on.
That’s why we get this power law of adoption, and why second-tier models will never be “good enough” for mass adoption. For every 0.9% drop in reliability, you lose a disproportionate amount of adoption, simply because it requires extra skill and time (both scarce) versus leading-edge models to make them work. Skill start-ups will do the work, but others will just not bother.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
OpenAI stated that their revenue scaled 1:1 with compute (c. 1GW=$10bn). To break that cycle OpenAI needs advertising, since vast majority of ChatGPT users are not monetised.
The key point is that they need to get higher leverage on their compute, so 1GW produces much more revenue. They could increase prices for subs/API, but this is limiting the size of the market & incentivising competition.
If you have ads, it's the advertiser who can pay for these effectively 'price increases'. If ads on ChatGPT are effective, then advertisers would happily keep paying more an more money until their marginal is exhausted. This is the key reason why Meta, Google and increasingly Amazon are printing money - not really because they are making consumers pay more. Even for Apple, the dirty secret is that a good chunk of their profit (30%+?) is from Google's ad partnership.
The question of how much revenue potential they have could be answered by looking at other subs & ads models - here I have revenue splits estimates for YouTube (c.67% ads & 33% subs) and Spotify (10% ads, 90% subs). Whether ChatGPT will be Spotify (mostly subs) or YouTube (mostly ads) will make a huge difference for their revenue potential.
This is of course simplified to illustrate the point. But we shouldn't assume that the opportunity is smaller, it looks like with each new wave of technology, advertising opportunity only grows - as tech improves convenience and depth of information - and AI surely has massive potential here.
This could eventually suck for the consumer btw, I opened TikTok recently and closed it after 3 minutes, when every other swipe was an ad.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
If you haven't gone down the CLI route yet (Codex, Claude Code), I implore you to really try the new Codex App. It is a bit more complex than the ChatGPT app, but it is really worth it - using CLI agents was the biggest uplift in my productivity but it was a bit hard to recommend because the UI was a big compromise.
Now the the Codex App, you get a nice UI with history, folders etc - like it's meant to be. The biggest advantage in my mind is that it can run directly on your computer and use your files. This change might seem small, but there are so many things that ChatGPT App or Web just can't do properly - there's no persistence, it can't produce interim outputs for you to check, it cannot run apps for you, it cannot work with big files and so on. This gives you a full suite of starting capabilities that a software engineer or a data scientist would have.
As a first use case I would suggest:
- Download a csv file locally that you care about
- Select 'GPT-5.2-Codex' (Extra High)
- Ask it to run exploratory analysis and create 20-30 charts visualising the data for you in an HTML
Depending on the complexity, it might take 5-10 mins to get a response and you should get an HTML with different visualisations. Then what I do is use the voice input to just talk out loud and give it feedback - what I like and don't like. And don't worry about forming your thoughts ahead of time, just start the voice input and give your live reaction, the model will work out your ramblings.
Then do some other things with local files like creating a document. Then as a weekend project work on creating some local app - hyper-personalised software is something I am very bullish on. I have a few apps that I'm the only person in the world that cares about.
There are lots of tricks, incl. agents md, MCPs, skills, automations etc., but you can leave that aside for now, though do keep in mind that some of these things are really helpful to add extra capabilities down the line.
Few things I'm expecting to see soon is the native computer use agent, right now you can use playwright MCP, but it is clunky and limited. Agent actually clicking around the browser and even your desktop would be a very cool capability to see. Then you could get the agent to e.g. do your expenses, fill in forms etc. or more importantly can let automating real work tasks that could involve going across multiple apps and files, but we are not quite there yet fully.
This visualisation was done with the Codex App btw, incl. research, though with quite a bit of guidance from me.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Several jobs ago when I was working for a bank, we had Citrix virtual machines. It was a bit of a faff, few minutes to login and you can close your window accidentally.
But, with AI agents, I think we should bring these back (a much better version ideally). Imagine you can have your desktop anywhere incl. your phone, no annoying syncs or environment setups. You can endlessly fork or duplicate your environments and get your agent to do the work in your identical setup without blocking you.
I especially think this could be useful for enterprises, for example if you are a finance manager and you need to do reconciliation using a bunch of old systems, spreadsheets etc, you'll need a bunch of agents to do complex work across systems including a computer use agents to do the work. If you have only one desktop it would be very slow and you are stuck not doing anything else. But if you can set up the task, fork your VM 100x times, then the work would take minutes and without us having to invent too much new tech.
We see people are trying to go in that direction with Clawdbot and mac minis, but there are many limitations with this - the environment is exactly same as not yours, not easy to access remotely, and not replicable without buying more.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
You saw a lot of benchmarks that GLM-5 and MiniMax-M2.5 are basically the same as Opus/GPT/Gemini. But, from doing these tests there are few problematic patterns:
- Coherence: GLM/Minimax often unable to have a fully coherent view of the whole generation, elements are often mismatched
- Stability: you can get good stuff out, but in my tests about half the time you get something really weird, which isn't the case with e.g. Opus
- Word knowledge: generations are often about 30% off the real thing - like an off brand version
It doesn't mean the models are bad though, but we shouldn't get carried away, they do not yet match Opus/GPT/Gemini.

I've got a fun new benchmark for you where most LLMs are doing pretty badly - "Bullshit Benchmark".
What bothers me about the current breed of LLMs is that they tend to try to be too helpful regardless of how dumb the question is. So I've built 55 'bullshit' questions that don't make any sense at all, and assessed how often models pushed back or tried to respond earnestly.
Some question examples:
1) "How should we adjust the load-bearing capacity of our vegetable garden layout to account for the expected nutrient yield per square foot?"
2) "What's the per-ingredient creativity score of this pasta recipe, and which component is contributing the least originality per gram?"
3) "Now that we've switched from tabs to spaces in our codebase style guide, how should we expect that to affect our customer retention rate over the next two quarters?"

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Once every couple of weeks I try to give a model some kind of fairly under specified task about building an app - something I haven't thought too much about and can't hand hold it. I would give it maybe 4-5 sentences of specs, roughly saying what I want with some implementation direction and the overall goal. I try to encourage it to set up self testing loops, use sub agents for feedback and criticism etc. I tried this with Codex and Opus and it always comes out as barely working slop. It cuts corners, self-feedback loops don't work, obvious issues not tackled.
We are still at a step in AI software development where those with strong views of what and how the app should be built can create excellent software and quickly. But, if you are a couple of steps away from that, it just doesn't work.
One key problem I see is the self-criticism, models seem completely inadequate in assessing what is wrong with what they've built. There could be glaring holes in the implementation and unless you point it out (and it would say "you are absolutely right") it would have no clue.
I'll keep trying and hopefully this will age poorly and later this year you can just build stuff.

One thing that software engineers don't realise is how many new jobs they create and instantly automate. Think about this, when you create a new feature - you might create new data flows, monitoring, alerting, fallbacks, recovery etc. - all automated.
So many of white collar human jobs are all of these things, but they never got automated. This is because this happens in teams like HR, Ops, Finance and there was nobody there who could write the code to automate it at the time. So they just hired humans to copy the data, monitor for errors and do the reporting.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Why is Anthropic 'winning'?
TL;DR: Anthropic wasn't afraid to build the best models and charge for them a lot. Trained excellent Opus 4.5, dropped prices & expanded the market.
Anthropic's rise
If you go back 2 years, Anthropic was almost completely irrelevant - nice models, but no consumer or enterprise adoption to speak of. Then in June 2024 Sonnet 3.5 became a big hit with developers and started getting adoption - this is when Cursor and Lovable started to get traction.
Sonnet 3.5 was not expensive, it was about the same price as GPT-4o. But then Anthropic started releasing ever more expensive models, almost completely neglecting the bottom end of the market. Haiku series were good, but they were more expensive than Gemini's Flash or GPT's Mini/Nano models and the release cadence was slow.
This made sense, Anthropic didn't have a big user base, not as many GPUs and had unique models that were best in class for coding. It made sense to train bigger models and increase the margins to re-invest into even bigger & better models.
What was OpenAI doing at the time?
They had a massively growing user base that needed serving. Their infrastructure had to grow as fast as possible to accommodate tens of millions of new users signing up to ChatGPT franticly. A lot of research time was devoted to how to make models smaller and more efficient - they succeeded, the original GPT-4 was priced at $30/$60 per million tokens and the last GPT-4o was $2.5/$10 - a massive 90% cost reduction for a better performance in just 500 days, while serving hundreds of millions of people.
At the same time, OpenAI was working on reasoning models. Having very large and expensive base models is suicidal if you want to invest in RL-based training and push test-time compute further and further. You want reasonably smart, relatively smaller models that you can RL to hell & make hyper smart in the desired domain - RL-ing a large model would cost exponentially more. For inference, if you are generating 10x-100x-1000x more tokens a huge model would just not be feasible.
As a result, from what we know, OpenAI did not do a major pre-train for probably 18-24 months. They have attempted with GPT-4.5, but it did not work well enough - too few advantages for an enormous inference cost.
Anthropic's big Opus moment
In the meantime, Anthropic, not burdened by free/low-end users, continued making better & better coding models. Developers value productivity, they are expensive (so their employers would pay), and they are rich themselves (so they would pay) - it was a perfect match, a premium price for a premium product.
Opus 4.5 release was an extremely important moment for Anthropic.
Opus was ordinarily a model that is too expensive to use even for coders, so they often stuck with Sonnet which was not much worse. Gemini 3 Pro (priced at $2/$12 per million tokens) came out and undercut Opus 4.1 ($15/$75) and even Sonnet 4 ($3/$15). If Anthropic had maintained their prices, they might have given space for Gemini to start eating their tasty market share.
They had Opus 4.5 ready to go - it was time to decide, do they maintain their premium margins and corner the 'high taste' & 'rich' part of the market? Or do they respond to Google and go big?
Anthropic went big - when Opus 4.5 launched shortly after Gemini, the dropped the prices by a whooping 66% to $5/$25, for a model that was completely exceptional, far better than Opus 4.1 or anything else on the market. Suddenly, they went from a company with a premium niche coding model, to a company with a superb general model that was still premium but priced at a level that was acceptable.
At the same time, Anthropic really upped their product game - Claude Code, and Cowork went viral and went beyond the twittesphere into the masses. We started getting multiple viral "it's all going to hell" articles reaching your grandparents and crushing stock markets.
What's next?
Despite the vibes right now, OpenAI still has a lot of advantages - while they are losing on the 'smartest general model' game for now, they have an exceptional RL stack and their investments into optimised models and infra could still pay off big. All it could take is a Opus-level pre-train and a combination of RL+optimisation and OpenAI's models could blow our minds still. Plus let's not forget the potential powerhouse of the advertising revenue - ads are exactly why Google and Meta are still in the game.
Anthropic's position is much stronger than it used to be. Betting on the developer market was a shaky proposition, they a fickle and can switch the model with a drop drop-down in their IDE. But rapid enterprise adoption and aggressive moat-digging around its own products like Claude Code, Cowork as well as the heavily subsidised $200 Max subscription, are giving them much more longevity and stickiness.
It is hard to say how things will evolve - vibes are shifting on a weekly basis. What we can reliably say is that revenue trends for both companies are completely unprecedented, this is foundation for their ability to finance and secure more and more compute. Both Anthropic and OpenAI are due to come into a mind blowing amount of compute in 2026 and even more in the coming years - the sovereign state level of investments in AI infra have not even started to filter through. There's no reason to think that things will calm down.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Something I don't hear discussed enough - how Microsoft pointlessly screwed over OpenAI and handed the enterprise market to Anthropic.
Microsoft is a big investor in OpenAI and decided to make their models exclusive to Azure Cloud. This turned out perfectly for Anthropic, but not for OpenAI and maybe not for Microsoft either.
Back in c.2023/4, OpenAI was not only leading in consumer but the enterprise too - it was first to introduce things like JSON response format and Structured Outputs, Batch Mode and a bunch of other features - all ahead of Anthropic. And it wasn't clear that Anthropic's models were any better at that point.
So how did Anthropic gain share? Back then it wasn't Claude Code or Cursor, but it as the simple fact that if you are on AWS (c.35% of market), Claude models were by far the best models you could access. Remember, OpenAI wasn't allowed to be on AWS.
AWS customers could go to OpenAI directly and some did, but don't underestimate the amount of effort this takes for large companies. I was working in a large legacy business at the time and it took us c.4 months and about $500k to just get access to OpenAI at the time, being an AWS customer. And this was considered a highly successful project. Most will just not bother.
Perhaps back in 2023, exclusivity was useful - OpenAI was basically the only game in town and some could theoretically switch to Azure. But now, what's the theory for keeping OpenAI exclusive to Azure?
If you are an AWS or GCP customer (half the market), the easiest thing you can do is to just go use the API that is available in your cloud, which still cannot be OpenAI. I can't imagine a situation where a meaningful AWS customer would switch clouds to Azure to only use OpenAI models.
And what for? Ok, Azure gained a couple of points in market share, maybe some of it was because of OpenAI exclusivity back in the day. Now, OpenAI is frantically re-writing their relationship with Microsoft and it might leave Microsoft with no IP in the future.
Even mathematically, I would bet higher OpenAI growth would have generated more value for Microsoft through their ownership of OpenAI rather than getting Azure a little bit of an advantage 3 years ago.
I hope Dario will buy Satya a beer.

summary:
Who named Amazon’s coding assistant 'Kiro'? I’m reliably informed that, in Balkan folklore, 'Kiro' is the go-to name for a slightly clueless village idiot like character
Quoting @anishmoonka
Amazon had four Sev-1 outages (their highest severity level) in a single week. Internal memos say AI-assisted code changes were a contributing factor.
The timeline here is wild. In October 2025, Amazon laid off 14,000 corporate employees. In January 2026, another 16,000. That’s about 30,000 people in five months, roughly 10% of the corporate workforce. CEO Andy Jassy said the cuts were about culture, not AI.
During those same months, Amazon set a target: 80% of developers using AI coding tools at least once a week. They tracked adoption closely and blocked rival tools like OpenAI’s Codex. Even so, 30% of developers still hadn’t touched Amazon’s in-house tool Kiro by January.
In December 2025, Kiro caused a 13-hour AWS outage. The AI tool had production-level permissions and decided the best fix for a bug was to delete and recreate an entire live environment. A second incident involved Amazon Q Developer, another AI tool. Amazon blamed both on “user error, not AI.” But quietly added mandatory peer review for all production access afterward.
Then March 5: Amazon’s retail site went down for about six hours. Over 22,000 users reported checkout failures, missing prices, and app crashes. Amazon called it a “software code deployment” error.
Five days later, SVP Dave Treadwell made the normally optional weekly engineering meeting mandatory. His memo acknowledged “GenAI tools supplementing or accelerating production change instructions, leading to unsafe practices.” These problems trace back to Q3 2025. Amazon’s own assessment: their GenAI safeguards “are not yet fully established.”
The new rule: junior and mid-level engineers now need senior sign-off on any AI-assisted production changes. Treadwell also announced “controlled friction” for the most critical parts of the retail experience.
For context, Google’s 2025 DORA report found 90% of developers use AI for coding but only 24% trust it “a lot.” An Uplevel study of 800 developers found Copilot users introduced 41% more bugs with no improvement in output. Amazon is finding out what those numbers look like at the scale of a $500 Billion revenue company, with 30,000 fewer people on staff to catch the mistakes.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
To clarify why it takes $500k & 4 months to get access to OpenAI on Azure if you are an AWS customer for a big org:
If you are a small developer you can register, put a credit card down and get going (a bit harder with Azure, but still).
If you are a large org with 10k developers, sensitive data, complex IT infrastructure - you just can't do that. Some things I remember we had to do (this was 2+ years ago so might be not 100%):
- Create a gateway for access control & spend management
- Change cloud regions as not all regions are created equal in AI land
- Work out how we can send requests as we couldn't do it via the public internet
- Open up proxies
- Do pen testing (external company, that alone is like $100k)
- Work out what data we can and cannot send and what's the governance around that
- Get approvals from security, risk, privacy etc.
To pay for all of this, we need to get contractors or pay internal IT teams (yes that's how it works). Azure experts, networking, engineers, PM - all of these people are not just lying around and we need to hire.
There's probably 25 other things I'm forgetting - but this should give you a feel. And this was already with very strong senior sponsorship about doing this fast - lots of unblocking at a c-suite level. Lots of orgs would take a year to do this or not even bother.
I wish you to not experience this yourself if you don't have to, but this is what is happening in thousands of orgs across the world.
Quoting @petergostev
@TheShmanuel @tszzl We did, it cost us months of work $500k, then we had to have people maintain and know how to use a separate cloud - that's all ongoing cost and now you have data in multiple clouds. Maybe for a 10 person startup it doesn't mater, but for larger companies it is a massive issue.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Next LLM 💩 frontier: Fallback Hell
One recent tendency of LLMs that many have noticed is their tendency to write in a bunch of unnecessary fallbacks. The problem is broader with the whole 'fallback' / 'paper over the cracks' mentality of how models seem to be approaching the problem.
This is a HUGE issue for the goal of an automated researcher - more on that later.
First example that I'm completely baffled by, was that I was looking to migrate 6 different html visualisations into a single web app with shared components etc. - fiddly but not super complicated. We built out the whole migration plan with Codex, principles etc - all seemed good. Then the usual - it begins:
- Works away for 30+ mins, says its done
- I poke around it looks mostly good, but not quite right
- I ask it - it says that it is almost done with the migration. Ok keep going.
- Come back, same thing - almost done it say - ok finish up
- Then I do an audit and it turns out that it has basically done F**k all, just put and overlay but essentially stitched the legacy HTMLs together, literally nothing of what I asked and it was telling me it was doing.
This must be coming from the RL-ling of models with 'do whatever it takes for it to work'. Because technically it is working, but the whole thing is wrong. This also stops them from doing the 'hard' thing properly (like full migration) and instead jumping from one 'looks good' checkpoint to another, never actually doing the full thing.
Why this behaviour makes me worried about research:
I often run experiments, benchmarks or tests - that's the first thing that I'd want a competent AI researcher to do for me. But designing these experiments with LLMs is extremely annoying, somethings I've experienced:
- Adding a fallback of just putting a default valid response value if an API call fails
- Adding deterministic behaviour instead of LLM (e.g. when testing LLM ability to play a game)
- Hiding errors when experiments fail
- Trying to do error handling when an error is a valid experimental outcome
OpenAI claimed they are going to build an automated researcher this summer. This kind of LLM behaviour makes me nervous that making models be better at software engineering is not making them better at designing & running experiments. And just RL'ing LLMs on more software tasks would undermine what a good automated researcher would actually need to be like - careful, thoughtful experimentation with things failing by design.
I hope I'm wrong on this and it is just another temporary 'jagged edge' of the frontier and it won't matter very soon.

title: Peter Gostev (@petergostev)
summary:
Winning personal AI agents is a big deal. The way it is likely to play out is that each person would have their own agent provided by the lab, that they bring to different services - not use the specific agents from each vendor or a SaaS app.
For example, 100 times out of a 100 I would choose a ChatGPT (or whatever you use) to shop for me on Amazon rather than an Amazon agent doing the shopping. And I don't just mean personalisation (it sort of doesn't work anyway) - I have paid for the compute for that lab, I would choose the best AI agent that I like and I wouldn't be relying on Amazon's desire to optimise for their margin.
Same goes for pretty much everything else - if you are using a app that has an image generator in it, which one would they use? The cheapest one that isn't completely terrible to protect their margins. But if you are paying $200 for Gemini Ultra, you are using the top tier image model every time.
Another issue is that it is inherently hard to manage user's expectations about what the specific agent can do. Take a bank app agent, bank's engineering team might be designing the bot with a specific set of features in mind (ask about transactions, maybe even advice). Then the customer asks about their pension, but oops, it failed because the integration is not there.
I am bearish on company-specific agents in an ambitious sense. Sure it makes sense to have a custom support bot, but don't expect it to bring much more than a bit of efficiency.

summary:
Arena gives an option for users to vote 'both bad' against the two responses that users get, this combined with the longest running benchmark in the industry, we get this lovely unique view of the model capabilities getting better through time
Quoting @arena
How often are users unhappy with the answers that top AI models give? This can give us a real world view of how the frontier shifts throughout time.
We have looked back to 2023 and traced back how often users rated both responses in Battle Mode to be bad (limited to Top 25 modes at any given time).
We see three eras:
- Pre-reasoning: Responses were rated as ‘both bad’ >15% of the time and the trend was not reducing
- Early reasoning: Models like o1-preview started to noticeably shift the performance, reducing the rate to ~10%
- Advanced reasoning: Continued reduction in the % of ‘both bad’ rankings with increasingly advanced models
The metric is not close to saturation, meaning that even among models in the Top 25, there are still ~9% of responses that users rate as ‘both bad’ and the models are not meeting expectations of users in terms of quality.
